title: Story points, magic estimation, PBS and PFD
blurb: Tell apart the plans practice techniques: story points and card-based estimating, magic estimation, the product breakdown structure and the product flow diagram.
question: Early in a project, a team must size dozens of epics quickly; later it needs to show which products must be finished before others can start. Which plans practice techniques fit each need?

teach.h: Estimate relatively, as a whole team
teach.body: The plans practice techniques in PRINCE2 Agile include the product breakdown structure, the product flow diagram, estimation and release planning. For estimation, the core idea is to use relative estimates rather than actual ones, and to draw on the knowledge of the whole team so everyone contributes without being swayed by others. The most common form is story points: a value that means something relative to another story.

teach.h: Plans practice techniques at a glance
head: Technique
What it does
Book
rows: Quick sizing of many items early
Releases shown on the release map

items: The team looks at one user story and its acceptance criteria.
Each team member picks a points value privately, on a pre-numbered card or paper.
Everyone reveals at the same moment, so nobody is swayed.
Differences are discussed and the team settles on a shared value.

teach.body: Magic estimation is a quick, collaborative technique used in early planning, for example at the level of the project product. It estimates the relative size or complexity of many pieces of work or user stories without lengthy discussion. Later, the detailed estimation of work happens in managing product delivery, in the effort estimation topic of each team planning workshop.

A product breakdown structure describes the products to be delivered and their essential components: each product is divided hierarchically into component elements and their requirements are collected. Building it helps identify dependencies, which a product flow diagram then shows: the sequence in which products will be developed and the dependencies between them. In agile planning a user story map is recommended in place of the PBS, but both techniques remain available.

Larchmont is refurbishing a branch and adding self-service kiosks. In initiation, project manager Owen Pritchard's teams use magic estimation to size 40 epics in under an hour. The physical refit is broken down with a PBS, and a PFD shows the layout must be approved before lighting is installed. In each team planning workshop, the kiosk software team sizes stories with pre-numbered cards, revealing at once, then plans the iteration.

teach.text: PBS = what the products and their parts are. PFD = the order products are developed and their dependencies. Magic estimation = fast relative sizing of many items early. Story points = relative values per story, not hours. Delegation poker sounds similar but belongs to the organization practice: it agrees decision-making levels, not sizes.

items: PRINCE2 Agile estimates relatively, using the whole team (8.4.3).
Story points: a value meaningful relative to other stories.
Card-based estimating: private choice, simultaneous reveal, then discussion.
Magic estimation: quick, collaborative sizing of many items in early planning.
PBS: products broken hierarchically into components (8.4.1).
PFD: sequence of development and dependencies (8.4.2).

summary: You can now distinguish story points, card-based estimating and magic estimation, and say when each fits. You can also explain what a product breakdown structure and a product flow diagram show, and how they relate in agile planning.

A.q: Which technique shows the sequence in which products will be developed and the dependencies between them?
options: Product breakdown structure
Product flow diagram
User story map
Burn-up chart
A.why: A product flow diagram illustrates the sequence of product development and the dependencies between products (8.4.2).

whyNot.0: A PBS breaks products into components; it helps find dependencies but does not show the sequence.
whyNot.2: A story map orders user activities and breaks them into stories, not product dependencies.
whyNot.3: A burn-up chart shows completed work against a deadline (progress practice).

A.q: Which technique is a quick, collaborative way to estimate the relative size of many user stories in early planning?
options: Magic estimation
Product flow diagram
Delegation poker
Velocity tracking
A.why: Magic estimation is a quick, collaborative technique for early planning that sizes many items without lengthy discussion (8.4.3).

whyNot.1: A PFD shows sequence and dependencies, not sizes.
whyNot.2: Delegation poker agrees levels of decision-making in the organization practice.
whyNot.3: Velocity measures points delivered per timebox; it does not size stories.

A.q: What does a product breakdown structure describe?
options: Who decides what within each of the delivery teams
The order of tasks for the team's next iteration
The story points completed per iteration
The products to be delivered and their components
A.why: A PBS describes the products to be delivered and their essential components, divided hierarchically (8.4.1).

whyNot.0: Decision authority is shown in a delegation matrix.
whyNot.1: The order of tasks for an iteration is in the team plan.
whyNot.2: Points completed per iteration describe velocity.

B.q: What is the principal idea behind estimation in PRINCE2 Agile?
options: Actual hours set by the most expert member
Fixed estimates approved by the project board
Relative estimates drawing on the whole team
Cost estimates prepared by project support
B.why: Book 8.4.3: use relative, not actual, estimates and harness the knowledge of the whole team.

whyNot.0: Actual estimates from one expert are what the technique moves away from.
whyNot.1: The board sets tolerances; it does not fix story estimates.
whyNot.3: Estimates come from the team doing the work, not from project support.

B.q:
Which two statements about plans practice techniques are correct?
1. Story points measure the hours a story will take.
2. A user story map is recommended in place of a PBS in agile.
3. A product flow diagram shows who is accountable for each product.
4. Developing a PBS helps identify dependencies between products.
options: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
B.why: Statements 2 and 4 are correct (8.3.1.1, 8.4.1, 8.4.2). Story points are relative values, and a PFD shows sequence and dependencies.

whyNot.0: Statement 1 is false: story points are relative values, not hours.
whyNot.1: Both are false: points are not hours, and a PFD shows sequence and dependencies, not accountability.
whyNot.3: Statement 3 is false: accountability is defined by the organization practice.

B.q: Story points are BEST described as:
options: the hours a developer needs to finish a story
a value meaningful relative to other stories
the cost of a story within the budget
a priority rank assigned using MoSCoW
B.why: Story points give a points value that means something relative to another requirement or story (8.4.3).

whyNot.0: Hours are actual estimates; points are relative.
whyNot.3: MoSCoW sets priority; story points set relative size.

C.q: A delivery team estimates the effort for each user story before choosing what to deliver in the next iteration. In which process does this happen, and what kind of estimate is used?
options: Initiating a project; actual estimates
Controlling a stage; actual estimates
Managing a stage boundary; relative estimates
Managing product delivery; relative estimates
C.why: Estimation of work takes place in managing product delivery (team planning workshop) and uses relative estimates (8.4.3, Table 13.13).

whyNot.0: Initiation plans at a high level, and PRINCE2 Agile prefers relative, not actual, estimates.
whyNot.1: Controlling a stage is the PM's process, and the estimates are relative.
whyNot.2: The estimate type is right, but iteration-level estimating happens in managing product delivery.

C.q: A project must size 60 epics quickly during initiation, and later each team sizes its stories every iteration. Which pair of techniques fits, in that order?
options: Magic estimation, then card-based story points
Card-based story points, then magic estimation
A product flow diagram, then a PBS
Delegation poker, then magic estimation
C.why: Magic estimation suits fast sizing of many items in early planning; card-based story point estimating suits each team planning workshop (8.4.3).

whyNot.1: This reverses the two: magic estimation is the quick early technique for many items.
whyNot.2: PFD and PBS describe products and their dependencies; they do not size stories.
whyNot.3: Delegation poker agrees decision-making levels, not sizes.

C.q: Which two techniques are linked because developing the first helps identify the dependencies shown in the second?
options: Story points and velocity
Story map and project canvas
PBS and product flow diagram
Burn-down and burn-up charts
C.why: Developing the PBS helps identify dependencies among products, which the product flow diagram describes (8.4.1, 8.4.2).

whyNot.0: Velocity is calculated from points delivered; neither shows product dependencies.
whyNot.1: The project canvas is the business case; the story map is not linked to it this way.
whyNot.3: Burn charts show progress, not product dependencies.

reteach.title: Parts list, assembly order, and a quick guess
reteach.question: Building flat-pack furniture, what helps more: a list of parts, the order you fit them in, or a rough guess of how big each job is?

blocks.body: A product breakdown structure is the parts list. A product flow diagram is the assembly order. Story points and magic estimation are ways of sizing the work relative to other work: magic estimation for lots of items fast and early, card-based points for each story as an iteration is planned.

blocks.text: None of these techniques measures hours: PRINCE2 Agile estimates relatively.

explain.body: PRINCE2 Agile estimates relatively, not in actual hours, and harnesses the whole team so nobody is swayed by others.

test.q: What kind of estimates does PRINCE2 Agile recommend?
options: Relative estimates rather than actual ones
Actual estimates rather than relative ones
Estimates set by the project manager
Top-down estimates from the project board
test.why: Book 8.4.3 recommends relative, not actual, estimates made with the whole team.

whyNot.2: Estimates should harness the whole team, not one person.
whyNot.3: The board sets tolerances; it does not estimate stories.

explain.body: A quick, collaborative technique used in early planning, such as at project product level, to size many items without lengthy discussion.

test.q: At which point is magic estimation especially useful?
options: At project closure, to size any defects still open
During daily stand-ups, to size each task in turn
In team retrospectives, to rate the team's mood
In early planning, such as at project product level
test.why: Magic estimation is used in early planning stages, for instance at the project product level (8.4.3).

whyNot.0: Closure confirms acceptance and handover; it is not when sizing is done.
whyNot.1: Stand-ups share daily progress and blockers; they are not sizing sessions.
whyNot.2: Retrospectives reflect on the iteration; they do not size work.

explain.body: Each product is divided hierarchically into its component elements, and the requirements for those elements are collected.

test.q: In a product breakdown structure, how is each product divided?
options: Chronologically into user activities
Hierarchically into component elements
By iteration into team tasks
By likelihood into threats
test.why: A PBS divides each product hierarchically into its component elements (8.4.1).

whyNot.0: Ordering user activities in time is how a story map is built.
whyNot.2: Tasks per iteration are in the team plan.
whyNot.3: Threats are assessed in the risk practice.

explain.body: Shows the sequence in which the products will be developed and the dependencies between them.

test.q: What does a product flow diagram show?
options: The breakdown of products into parts
The size of each product in points
The owner of each product backlog
Development sequence and dependencies
test.why: A product flow diagram illustrates the sequence of product development and the dependencies between products (8.4.2).

whyNot.0: Breaking products into parts is the PBS.
whyNot.1: Sizing in points is story point estimation.
whyNot.2: Backlog ownership is a role responsibility, not a planning diagram.
